title: Design a Chat App
subtitle: Send one message through persistent connections, storage, delivery receipts, group fan-out and offline sync.
learn: Why chat uses long-lived WebSocket connections and how a gateway tier scales them
How a message is stored first, then routed to the recipient's gateway
How sent, delivered and read receipts flow back as ordinary messages
How group fan-out cost grows with group size, and how presence stays affordable with batched heartbeats
How an offline user catches up using a per-conversation sequence number

steps.title: Alice texts Bob
steps.body: Alice types hi and presses send. Within a fraction of a second Bob's phone should buzz, Alice should see a tick, and nothing may be lost even if Bob's phone is off. Plain HTTP lets only the client start a request, so the server cannot speak first. How does it push a message to Bob the moment it arrives? Assume 100 million daily users sending about 40 messages each.
steps.idea: Chat needs server-initiated delivery, durability, and ordering, all at once.
steps.caption: Two phones, and a message that must cross the system.

steps.title: Keep a socket open
steps.body: Polling every second wastes millions of empty requests, and long-polling is only an older workaround. Instead each app opens a WebSocket: an ordinary HTTP request upgraded into a long-lived two-way channel. A gateway holds it, behind a load balancer. The gateway reports Alice as online, and the chat service records in a fast store that she is reachable through gateway A. With about 20 million users online and roughly 100,000 sockets per gateway, you need around 200 gateways. If one dies, its clients reconnect elsewhere with randomized backoff, and its stale routes expire on their own. Keep spare capacity beyond 200.
steps.idea: Gateways only hold connections; a route table says which gateway holds which user.
steps.caption: Socket opens and the route is recorded.

steps.title: Store first, then ack
steps.body: Alice's app sends the message with a client-generated ID over the socket. The chat service assigns the next sequence number for that conversation and writes the message durably before replying, along with a durable (conversation, message ID) record. Only then does Alice see the single tick. A retry after a dropped connection finds the ID and returns the original ack instead of storing a second copy.
steps.idea: Persist before acknowledging, and use a message ID so retries are safe.
steps.caption: Message saved, then Alice gets a sent tick.

steps.title: Where messages live
steps.body: At 46,000 messages a second, one database server cannot take the writes, so the store is sharded. Partition by conversation ID and order rows by sequence number, so one chat's history is a single range read. Every write for a conversation goes through one owner at a time, such as the shard leader or a per-conversation sequencer, which increments the counter and inserts the row only if that seq is free, so 4021 is never issued twice. Assume about 100 bytes of text payload; with IDs, timestamps and indexes budget 200-300 bytes, so 0.8-1.2 TB a day before replication. Media goes to separate blob storage. Plan retention.
steps.idea: One owner per conversation allocates seq; partition by conversation, order by seq.
steps.caption: Store is sharded by conversation, rows ordered by seq.

steps.title: Deliver, then receipts
steps.body: The chat service looks up Bob in the route table, finds gateway B, and queues the message for it; the gateway pushes it down his socket. A user can have several devices, so the route table holds a set of gateways per user. Delivery is at-least-once, so Bob's app drops duplicates by message ID. His phone then sends a delivered receipt, and later a read receipt: small messages that travel back to Alice's gateway through the same queue. One read receipt can cover everything up to seq 4021.
steps.idea: A route lookup plus a queue reaches any user, and receipts are small cursor messages (up to seq N) sent back the same way.
steps.caption: Message reaches Bob, receipts return as ticks.

steps.title: One message, many inboxes
steps.body: In a group of 500 people, one message must reach 499 others. The simplest design stores the message once under the group and queues the small message itself (text is tiny) for each member's gateway. The service looks up all 499 routes, groups them by gateway, and sends one batch per gateway. Storage stays flat, but delivery work grows with group size, and so do receipts: big groups usually show only an aggregate (read by 37) or skip per-member receipts. That is why apps cap group sizes; huge broadcast channels use a pull-based design.
steps.idea: Store once, deliver many: fan-out cost scales with members, not with storage.
steps.caption: One stored message becomes hundreds of deliveries.

steps.title: Bob's phone is off
steps.body: Replay the same send, but Bob's phone is off when m1 (seq 4021) arrives. Now Bob has no socket, so the route table has no entry for him. The message is already stored, so nothing is lost. The chat service asks the push provider to send a notification that wakes his phone. The push carries little or no content; it only says there is something new. Push is best effort and may be delayed or dropped. Presence can lag, so if no delivered receipt comes back within a few seconds, the service sends the push anyway.
steps.idea: The stored message is the truth; push is only a nudge to come and get it.
steps.caption: No route found, so a push nudge goes out.

steps.title: Catch up on reconnect
steps.body: Bob turns his phone on. It reconnects and sends the last sequence number it holds for each chat, say 4020. The server reads everything after that from the store and sends it in order. Sequence numbers make catch-up exact: no guessing from timestamps, which clocks can disagree on. The same path repairs any gap caused by a dropped delivery. If Bob receives seq 4023 right after 4021, he knows 4022 is missing and asks for it. Real apps often also keep a per-user inbox sequence (a changelog of which chats have news), so reconnect asks one question instead of one per chat.
steps.idea: Clients ask for everything after seq N, which makes sync idempotent and gap-free.
steps.caption: Bob pulls messages after his last known seq.

steps.title: Presence without a storm
steps.body: The green dot means a user is online. Each app sends a heartbeat every 30 seconds, and the route entry expires if two are missed, so crashes clean themselves up. Naively, 20 million users is about 670,000 refreshes a second; each gateway absorbs its sockets' heartbeats and sends one batched refresh every few seconds. Batching cuts round trips, not key writes; to cut writes too, a gateway can hold one lease key, and every route it owns counts as alive while that lease is renewed. The cost is that a dot can lag by up to about 70 seconds. Presence is fetched lazily, only for chats on screen.
steps.idea: Treat presence as soft, expiring state and publish it only to people looking.
steps.caption: Gateways batch heartbeats into short-lived presence entries.

steps.title: The whole path
steps.body: Persistent sockets on a gateway tier carry messages. The chat service stores each message with a sequence number, acks the sender, looks up the recipient's gateway, and delivers through a queue. Receipts flow back the same way, groups fan out from one stored copy, offline users get a push nudge and then sync by sequence number, and presence is soft, expiring state refreshed in batches.
steps.idea: Store first, route by lookup, and let sequence numbers repair every gap.
steps.caption: Every component and its job in one picture.

quiz.q: A gateway crashes while holding 100,000 sockets. What should the design guarantee about messages sent to those users?
options: They are lost, because the sockets died with the gateway
They stay in the store; clients reconnect and sync after their last seq
They are retried forever, but only by the sender's app
They are moved into the other gateways' memory automatically
quiz.why: Messages are persisted before being acked and delivery is only a nudge on top. After reconnecting to any gateway, each client asks for everything after its last sequence number.

quiz.q: Why does the chat service write the message to the store before sending the sent tick to Alice?
options: Writes are always faster than delivering to the recipient
So the message needs no client-generated ID at all
Because Bob must already be online to receive it
So a tick always means the message will not be lost
quiz.why: If the tick were sent first and the server then crashed, Alice would believe it was sent while no copy existed. Persisting first makes the ack a durable promise.

quiz.q: A group has 1,000 members and gets 5 messages per second. About how many deliveries per second must the system make, and what stays flat?
options: About 5,000 deliveries/s; only 5 stored writes/s
About 5 deliveries/s; stored writes grow to 5,000/s
About 1,000 deliveries/s; only 1 stored write/s
About 5,000 deliveries/s and 5,000 stored writes/s
quiz.why: Each message goes to roughly 1,000 recipients, so about 5,000 deliveries per second, but one stored copy per message keeps storage at 5 writes per second.

quiz.q: Bob was offline and the push notification never arrived. When does he get his messages?
options: Never, push is the only delivery route
When Alice resends them
When he next opens the app and syncs after his last seq
After the queue's retention expires
quiz.why: Push is best effort and only a hint. The authoritative path is the sync request on reconnect, which reads the stored messages by sequence number.

quiz.q: Why is presence implemented as heartbeats with a TTL instead of an online/offline event on every change?
options: Events cannot cross gateways at all
TTLs are required by the WebSocket protocol
It guarantees that messages arrive in order
Crashes send no offline event, and fanning every flap out is costly
quiz.why: A crashed phone cannot announce it left, so an expiring entry cleans itself up. Publishing every change to all contacts multiplies cost, so presence is fetched lazily.

cheatsheet.def: A long-lived two-way connection started by an HTTP upgrade, letting the server push data without the client asking.
Servers that only hold sockets (about 100k each as a rule of thumb) and forward messages; kept stateless apart from their connections.
A fast key-value map from user to the gateway holding their socket, with a TTL refreshed by heartbeats.
A per-conversation counter assigned on write. Gives ordering, gap detection, and exact catch-up with sync after N. Duplicates are dropped by message ID.
Delivery may repeat, so receivers drop duplicates by message ID. Easier and safer than trying for exactly-once.
One read or delivered marker meaning everything up to seq N, instead of a receipt per message.
Store a group message once and queue it for each member's gateway (looked up in the route table); cost grows with member count.
A best-effort wake-up through APNs or FCM for offline devices; never the source of truth.

lab.prompt: Design a one-to-one and group chat service for 100 million daily users (about 20 million online at peak). Sketch the components, the message path, and the data model, then say what happens when a gateway dies.
requirements: Messages from one sender in one conversation arrive in order
A message is never lost once the sender sees it as sent
Delivery to an online recipient in well under a second
Offline users receive everything when they return
Handle roughly 46,000 messages per second on average and 3x at peak
hints: Estimate gateway count from concurrent connections divided by sockets per server
Choose a partition key for storage so one conversation's messages sit together, ordered by sequence number
Decide what the ack means and when it is sent
Think about how a client detects a gap or a duplicate
Keep presence as expiring soft state rather than durable data
Estimate storage per day and per year, and decide retention
checklist: Persistent connection tier separated from the message-handling service
Route table from user to gateway with expiry
Storage partition key and how sequence numbers are allocated safely
Message stored with a per-conversation sequence number before the ack
Receipts defined as cursors that flow back along the same path
Group fan-out plan and a size limit
Offline path covering push and sync after last seq
Failure story for a dead gateway
